rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Asad reads muttaqī as awareness of God's all-presence and the wish to shape one's life by it; 'God-fearing' is too narrow, while guarding against evil captures only one aspect.
rows.anchor: the awareness of His all-presence and the desire to mould one's existence in the light of this awareness

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Andād is plural of nidd, literally 'compeers'; Asad says a free rendering is needed to convey the phrase's meaning.
rows.anchor: "do not give God any compeers" (andad, pl. of nidd )

rows.speaker: all commentators
rows.claim: Commentators agree that the term includes worshipped objects credited with divine qualities, whether deities in their own right or saints said to possess divine or semi-divine powers.
rows.anchor: There is full agreement among all commentators that this term implies any object of adoration

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Islam requires respect and protection for every God-centered religion's house of worship despite doctrinal disagreement; blocking others from worship is sacrilege.
rows.anchor: every religion which has belief in God as its focal point must be accorded full respect

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: As an illustration, the Prophet let the Christian deputation from Najran enter his mosque and perform its rites there, despite their beliefs about Jesus and Mary conflicting with Islam.
rows.anchor: They were given free access to the Prophet's mosque, and with his full consent celebrated their religious rites there

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Asad rejects the suggestion that this describes a particular contemporary of the Prophet, finding no valid reason for that identification.
rows.anchor: no valid reason to suppose, as some commentators do, that this refers to a particular person

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: He takes the passage generally, following the most reliable authorities, as contrasting people focused only on worldly life with those mindful of the hereafter too.
rows.anchor: the most reliable authorities hold that the above passage has a general meaning

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: The context makes this a further elaboration of the contrast between two attitudes introduced in 2:200–201.
rows.anchor: it is a further elaboration of the allusion, made in 2:200-201, to two contrasting attitudes

rows.speaker: Az-Zajjaj
rows.claim: Az-Zajjaj, as quoted by Razi, explains the phrase as someone adept at defeating opponents in controversy with extremely adroit, often misleading arguments.
rows.anchor: According to Az-Zajjaj (quoted by Razi), this signifies a person who is always able to defeat his opponent

words: وَيُشْهِدُ ٱللَّهَ عَلَىٰ مَا فِى قَلْبِهِۦ
rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Asad sees people with plausible social-improvement aims who exclude the hereafter and use apparently sound ethical arguments to justify exclusive concern with worldly affairs.
rows.anchor: people who hold plausible and even admirable views regarding a possible improvement of human society

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Asad says this mindset has an inescapable affinity with the attitude described in 2:8–12.
rows.anchor: There is an inescapable affinity between the mental attitude described in the above passage and the one spoken of in 2:8-12

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Most commentators infer conscious intent; Asad says li may instead mark consequence regardless of intent, and his rendering leaves both readings open.
rows.anchor: the particle li in li-yufsida (generally taken to mean "in order that he might spread corruption") plays in this context

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Harth primarily means gain or acquisition through labour, and can denote worldly goods, crops, or the cultivated land itself; 'tilth' can metaphorically mean human and social endeavours.
rows.anchor: its primary significance is "gain" or "acquisition" through labour; and thus it often signifies "worldly goods"

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Some commentators, citing 2:223, take harth here to mean wives, so destroying tilth and progeny means disrupting family life and the social fabric.
rows.anchor: some commentators - basing their opinion on the Qur'anic sentence, "your wives are your tilth" (2:223)- maintain that harth stands here for "wives"

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: On either reading, making this worldly-only attitude the basis of social behavior inevitably causes widespread moral decay and social disintegration.
rows.anchor: and made the basis of social behaviour, it unavoidably results in widespread moral decay

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: The phrase translated 'without remarrying' literally means 'by themselves'.
rows.anchor: Lit., "by themselves".

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: The waiting period establishes whether the wife is pregnant and the unborn child's parentage; it also gives the couple time to reconsider and resume the marriage.
rows.anchor: The primary purpose of this waiting-period is the ascertainment of possible pregnancy, and thus of the parentage of the as yet unborn child

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: A divorced wife may refuse resumed relations even if her husband rescinds the provisional divorce during the waiting period; because he maintains the family, he has the first option to rescind.
rows.anchor: A divorced wife has the right to refuse a resumption of marital relations even if the husband expresses, before the expiry of the waiting-period

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: In any dangerous situation where staying in one place increases peril, obligatory prayer may be performed in any feasible way, even without facing the qiblah.
rows.anchor: where remaining for any length of time at one place would only increase the peril: in such an event, the obligatory prayers may be offered

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: The requested burden recalls both the heavy ritual law imposed on the children of Israel and the world-renunciation Jesus recommended to his followers.
rows.anchor: the heavy burden of rituals imposed by the Law of Moses upon the children of Israel, as well as the world-renunciation recommended by Jesus

rows.speaker: Tabari
rows.claim: Tabari says Mary was entrusted to Zachariah, her relative and a Temple priest, after lots decided which priest would care for her because her mother's vow dedicated her to Temple service.
rows.anchor: the guardianship of Mary was entrusted to Zachariah - who was not only her relative but also a priest attached to the Temple - after lots had been drawn

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Against commentators' legends, Asad finds no Qur'anic or authentic-Tradition evidence that Mary's provisions were miraculous.
rows.anchor: there is no indication whatsoever either in the Qur'an or in any authentic Tradition that these provisions were of a miraculous origin

rows.speaker: Tabari
rows.claim: Tabari relates that when aged Zachariah could no longer support Mary, the community arranged for another member to provide her daily food; Asad leaves the story's authenticity unresolved.
rows.anchor: Tabari quotes a story to the effect that when, in his old age, Zachariah became unable to support Mary by his own means

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Asad reads Mary's answer as expressing her deep awareness that God is the ultimate Provider.
rows.anchor: Mary's answer to Zachariah reflects no more and no less than her deep consciousness of God as the ultimate Provider

rows.speaker: Muhammad 'Abduh
rows.claim: Abduh reads the aside to the Prophet as stressing that Mary's Qur'anic story comes directly through revelation and is inherently true despite differences from Christian scripture.
rows.anchor: authentic (Muhammad 'Abduh in Manar III, 301 f.).

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: The wording literally means 'they cast their reeds'; Asad sees it as an ancient Semitic lot-drawing custom, perhaps like pre-Islamic Arab divination with blunt arrows.
rows.anchor: The phrase rendered above as "they drew lots" reads literally, "they cast their reeds" - obviously a reference to an ancient Semitic custom

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: The pronoun 'they' refers to the priests, one of whom was Zachariah.
rows.anchor: The pronoun "they" relates to the priests, of whom Zachariah was one

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: The phrase literally means '[any] other than God's religion'.
rows.anchor: Lit., "[any] other than God's religion".

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: The final phrase literally means 'will be returned'; Asad directs readers to 13:15 for its explanation.
rows.anchor: Lit., "will be returned". For an explanation of this sentence, see 13:15

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: God lightens the human burden through guidance that reconciles spiritual and bodily impulses and brings both elements of human nature to full fruition.
rows.anchor: to remove, by means of His guidance, all possibility of conflict between man's spirit and his bodily urges

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Though the address directly names the Prophet, Asad says it also applies to everyone who accepts Qur'anic guidance, as the plural address in 4:109 shows.
rows.anchor: by implication, however, it is addressed to everyone who has accepted the guidance of the Qur'an

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Asad rejects most commentators' exclusively historical explanation as unconvincing because it needlessly limits a self-explanatory ethical teaching of general scope.
rows.anchor: the attempt on the part of most of the commentators to explain this passage in purely historical terms is not very convincing
